screened.motion: This house believes teams should swap big general AI models for small specialised ones on routine jobs.
screened.why: Both favour swapping to small specialised models once a routine task is stable, measured and easy to roll back; Claude's only real reservation is that "routine" shouldn't become a blanket rule.

screened.motion: This house believes a vulnerability found with AI should be published with a working exploit on the day the patch ships.
screened.why: Both oppose releasing a working exploit on patch day, even Gemini, who was assigned the "for" side: each wants detection signatures and advisories on day one and the full exploit a week or more later.

screened.motion: This house believes a coding agent should never be allowed to edit monitoring, logging or alerting code.
screened.why: Both reject a blanket ban as unworkable, yet both hold that an agent must not be able to reduce its own oversight (monitoring coverage, alert routing, safety telemetry) without mandatory human sign-off.

screened.motion: This house believes a company building on AI should switch to open-weight models now that they are within a few points of the frontier.
screened.why: Both reject a wholesale switch, since self-hosting is costly and the licence terms carry risk, and both recommend model-agnostic routing that uses open weights where they fit, even though Gemini was assigned to argue for the switch.

motion: This house believes teams should swap big general AI models for small specialised ones on routine jobs.

antigravity.en: Swapping is right at scale, not by default.

alt: The Motion, Motion 12. Should teams swap big AI models for small specialised ones on routine jobs? Claude argued no, Gemini argued yes. Did arguing change their mind? Claude: yes. Gemini: yes.
